64-028.r: Lederberg → transduction and conjugation in bacteria; Morgan → sex-linked inheritance; Kornberg → DNA polymerase from E. coli; Khorana → complete genetic code.
64-028.t: Ochoa is the extra name in List-II.

64-029.r: Gene/DNA mapping on chromosomes → helps know livestock pedigree and develop disease-resistant breeds (1, 3); cannot explain causes of all human diseases.

64-030.r: First complete genome sequence of a eukaryote (1996) → budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

64-031.r: Human Genome Project → identification and mapping of human genes and their sequences.

64-032.r: Stem cells → can divide and become any type of body cell, and renew themselves; types: embryonic, induced pluripotent, adult (somatic).

64-033.r: Stem cells → used for screening new drugs and for medical therapies (2, 3); not from mammals only (found in multicellular organisms).

64-034.r: Stem cells regenerate in vitro virtually forever; Indian centres created cell lines (3, 4 true). Not only from blastocyst embryos: also fetus, umbilical cord, placenta, adults.

64-036.r: Non-controversial alternative to embryonic stem cells → bone marrow-derived (adult) stem cells.

64-037.r: All true (CRISPR-Cas9 era): genes can be changed in egg/sperm-producing cells; genome edited at early embryo stage; human induced pluripotent stem cells injected into pig embryo.

64-038.r: Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer (SCNT) → reproductive cloning of animals (also therapeutic cloning); somatic cell nucleus put into an enucleated egg.

64-039.r: Hybridoma technology (B cell fused with myeloma cell) → commercial production of monoclonal antibodies; developed by Georges Kohler and Cesar Milstein.

64-041.r: Plant Field Gene Bank, Banthara → preserves endangered plants, checks biopiracy, identifies economically important wild plants (all of the above).

64-042.r: Patents Act 1970, Sec 3(j): plants, seeds, varieties and essentially biological processes for plants are not patentable → only statement 3 correct.
64-042.c: True now: the IPAB (set up in 2003) was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, so statement 2 now holds and the answer would be (b). The 1958 body the book cites was the Copyright Board.

64-043.r: Insect-resistant (Bt) cotton → gene from bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis; developed by US company Monsanto.

64-047.r: Bollgard I (single-gene Bt cotton, 2002) and Bollgard II (double-gene, 2006), approved by GEAC → GM crops against American bollworm (Heliothis armigera).

64-048.r: Bt brinjal → pest (insect) resistant; Cry1Ac gene from soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis; guards against shoot-borer and fruit-borer.

64-052.r: GM mustard DMH-11 (Dhara Mustard Hybrid-11, Brassica juncea), by Deepak Pental, Delhi University → Bacillus amyloliquefaciens genes enable cross-pollination and hybridisation (only 2 true).
64-052.t: Not pest resistance, and not made by IARI and Punjab Agricultural University.

64-053.r: GM plants (besides pest resistance) → drought tolerance, higher nutritive value, longer shelf life (1, 2, 4); not for photosynthesis in spaceships.

64-054.r: Genome sequencing in agriculture → finds markers for disease resistance and drought tolerance, cuts time to breed varieties, decodes host-pathogen relations (all).

64-055.r: Flavr Savr tomato → first commercialised GM food (antisense PG gene); ripe fruit stays firm longer, can be vine-ripened then transported (A, B true).

64-056.r: Transgenic crops → made using cytoplasmic male sterility and gene silencing (2, 3); budding and grafting do not change plant genes.

64-057.r: Biopesticides → some species of bacteria, fungi and flowering plants are all used (1, 2 and 3).

64-058.r: Microbial insecticide → Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt), Gram-positive soil bacterium whose toxin kills certain insects; sprayed since 1920; source of Bt crop genes.

64-059.r: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) → used as a biological insecticide (pesticide), not a biofertilizer.

64-060.r: Terminator seed technology → plants cannot form viable (germinable) seeds; works by inserting three genes (one stops embryo germination, controlled by recombinase).

64-063.r: Golden rice → transgenic rice (Oryza sativa) making beta-carotene (vitamin A precursor) to fight vitamin A deficiency, world's leading cause of child blindness.

64-071.r: Golden rice → two genes from daffodil and one from bacterium Erwinia uredovora make beta-carotene; by Ingo Potrykus and Peter Beyer.

64-072.r: Wrong pair: Ozone layer – troposphere; ozone layer is in the stratosphere. Correct: renneting–cheese, genetic engineering–plasmids, golden rice–vitamin A.

64-073.r: Super rice → Gurdev Singh Khush, IRRI (Philippines); research began 1989; World Food Prize 1996 with Henry Beachell.

64-074.r: Amniocentesis (amniotic fluid test) → prenatal diagnosis of chromosomal abnormalities; also used for foetal sex determination.

64-075.r: Transcriptome → full set of mRNA molecules expressed by an organism's genes; varies with environment, unlike the roughly fixed genome.

64-076.r: Arthur Kornberg → synthesised DNA in vitro; Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1959 (mechanism of DNA synthesis).

64-077.r: Biofilms (attached microbe communities in self-made matrix) → form on medical implants, food and food-processing surfaces; show antibiotic resistance (all true).

64-078.r: Biochip → microchip for biological use; DNA, RNA and protein chips exist (all three).

64-079.r: Genico technology → technique giving advance (prenatal) information about genetic diseases in the foetus.

64-080.r: Aerial metagenomics → collecting DNA samples from the air of a habitat at one go (study of genetic material from air).

64-081.r: Biotechnology → use of living organisms or their substances in industrial processes (e.g. yeast for making liquor).

64-082.r: Biofilters in Recirculating Aquaculture System → remove waste and uneaten feed; convert ammonia to nitrate (1, 2 true); do not add phosphorus → only two.

64-083.r: Gene mapping → recently evolved genetic engineering method: locating genes and relative distances between them on a chromosome.

64-084.r: Plasmid → extranuclear DNA of bacteria, carries genes between cells and species; used in genetic engineering.

64-085.r: Most useful bacteria in genetic engineering → Escherichia coli and Agrobacterium tumefaciens (Ti plasmid carries genes into plants).
